back_blocks.md: An **antibiotic** is a chemical, made by microorganisms, that **kills** or **inhibits the growth** of bacteria.

cards.back_md: An **antibiotic** is a chemical, made by microorganisms, that **kills** or **inhibits the growth** of bacteria.

back_blocks.md: It **prevents the synthesis of cross-links** in the bacterial **cell wall**.
The weakened wall cannot withstand the pressure as **water enters by osmosis**, so the cell **bursts (lysis)**.

front_blocks.md: Why does penicillin only affect **actively growing** bacteria?

back_blocks.md: Penicillin stops **new cell wall** material from forming.
Only dividing cells are building new wall, so cells that are **not growing** are unaffected.

back_blocks.md: Viruses have **no cell wall, ribosomes or metabolic machinery** of their own — they use the **host cell's**.
Antibiotics target **bacterial structures and processes** that viruses do not have.

front_blocks.md: Antibiotics can be used to treat HIV.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
HIV is a **virus**, and antibiotics only work against **bacteria**.

back_blocks.md: **Antibiotic resistance** is when bacteria are able to **survive exposure** to an antibiotic that would normally kill them.

cards.back_md: **Antibiotic resistance** is when bacteria are able to **survive exposure** to an antibiotic that would normally kill them.

front_blocks.md: How does antibiotic resistance **arise** in a population of bacteria?

back_blocks.md: A random **mutation** gives some bacteria a **resistance allele**.
When the antibiotic is used, resistant bacteria **survive and reproduce** (natural selection), so the resistant type becomes **more common**.

front_blocks.md: How can resistance genes **spread between** bacteria?

back_blocks.md: By the transfer of **plasmids** carrying the resistance gene (conjugation), so resistance can pass even between **different species** of bacteria.

front_blocks.md: Using antibiotics creates the mutations that make bacteria resistant.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Mutations occur **randomly**. The antibiotic does not cause them — it **selects for** bacteria that are already resistant.

front_blocks.md: What are the main **consequences** of antibiotic resistance?

back_blocks.md: Infections become **harder or impossible to treat**.
Illnesses last longer and spread more, causing **more deaths**, **higher healthcare costs**, and making routine **surgery riskier**.

cards.back_md:

front_blocks.md: What steps can **doctors and patients** take to reduce antibiotic resistance?

back_blocks.md: Only **prescribe antibiotics when necessary** (not for viral infections).
Always **finish the full course**, and use the **correct, specific antibiotic**.

front_blocks.md: Besides careful prescribing, what steps reduce the **spread** of resistance?

Colds and flu are caused by **viruses**, so antibiotics have no effect. Prescribing them only encourages **resistance**.
